quizzes.title: 20.5 Reading Quiz: The Dutch Republic
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in Week 20: The Dutch Republic. It has 7 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: Philip II tried to rule his empire by reading and answering reports in Madrid. Why did this habit weaken his hold on the Low Countries?

answers.text: His governors in Brussels were secretly loyal to the rebels and ignored the reports he sent them.
He had no silver to pay couriers, so reports reached him only once a year, if at all.
Answers to urgent questions took weeks to arrive, after events had changed.
He refused to read reports written by Protestant subjects, so he never heard their grievances.

questions.feedback_correct: Every important question traveled to Madrid by courier. A governor could watch a crisis grow but could not settle it without the king's word, and orders often arrived after the situation had changed.

questions.text: The Duke of Alba's rule united groups that had little reason to cooperate before. Which of his actions did the most to bring Catholics and Protestants, nobles and merchants, together against Philip?

answers.text: He executed Catholic nobles such as Egmont and Hoorn and taxed sales heavily.
He allowed Calvinist crowds to destroy statues and stained glass in the churches across the provinces.
He moved the seat of government from Brussels to Madrid, far from the people it ruled.
He cut the dikes around Leiden to drive the rebels out of the city, but the plan failed.

questions.feedback_correct: Alba's Council of Blood punished even loyal Catholics, and the new tax hit every town. Within a few years he had made enemies of nearly everyone in the provinces.

questions.text: In 1574 the people of Leiden were starving, yet the city was saved by flooding the countryside. Why did the flood help the rebels and not the Spanish?

answers.text: The water destroyed the Spanish fleet before it could reach the coast, ending the siege at sea.
The flood washed away Leiden's walls so that the rebel army could march straight into the city.
The Spanish soldiers could not swim and drowned in large numbers as the water rose around them.
Shallow rebel ships could sail over the drowned fields as the Spanish pulled back.

questions.feedback_correct: The Dutch used their old knowledge of dikes in a new way. The rising water gave the rebel ships a path to the walls and forced the besiegers to withdraw.

questions.text: William of Orange was killed by an assassin in 1584, but the revolt did not collapse. Which explanation best fits the lesson?

answers.text: Philip II called off the war at once because he feared the growing power of the Dutch navy.
Maurice rebuilt the army, and provincial councils kept governing.
The Catholic southern provinces took over the fighting and drove the Spanish out by 1585.
The English king sent an army across the sea that finished the war within a few years.

questions.feedback_correct: The revolt had leaders and institutions beyond one man. Maurice rebuilt the army, and each province kept its own councils and stadtholder, so the cause outlived William.

questions.text: In 1576 Spanish soldiers sacked Antwerp and killed thousands of its people, though Philip had not ordered it. What does the lesson suggest was the underlying cause?

answers.text: Antwerp had refused to pay its taxes to the Spanish crown for several years in a row.
William of Orange had hidden his army inside the city, and the Spanish moved to dislodge it.
The soldiers went unpaid after Philip's bankruptcy and mutinied.
Alba had ordered an example to be made of Protestant cities that had joined the rebels.

questions.feedback_correct: Philip's wars cost more than his silver could cover. His government went bankrupt in 1575, his unpaid soldiers mutinied, and the sack of Antwerp followed.

questions.text: Hugo Grotius argued that the sea was open to the ships of every nation. Yet the Dutch East India Company often shut out rivals once its own ships controlled a trade. What does this suggest?

answers.text: The Dutch used the principle when it helped and dropped it when it did not.
The company had never heard of Grotius's argument and acted entirely on its own.
Grotius's pamphlet was written to defend Portugal and its claim to the Asian trade.
The company had lost interest in trade and wanted only to rule islands as a government.

questions.feedback_correct: The company liked the argument when it was breaking Portugal's hold on Asian trade. After it controlled a trade of its own, it often excluded competitors.

questions.text: Why was the joint-stock structure of the Dutch East India Company so useful for raising money?

answers.text: The government promised to repay every investor's losses if a fleet failed to return home.
Anyone could buy a share, risk only what was invested, and resell it at the bourse.
Only the richest merchants of Amsterdam were allowed to own shares, so the company faced no risk.
Investors received spices directly in place of money, so no cash had to change hands.

questions.feedback_correct: Limited risk and resalable shares let ordinary savers invest. They no longer had to wait years for a fleet to come home to get their money back.

quizzes.title: 22.5 Reading Quiz: England: Crown and Parliament
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in Week 22: England: Crown and Parliament. It has 7 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: Charles I ruled for eleven years without calling Parliament, and he raised money through ship money. John Hampden refused to pay it, and the judges ruled for the king by only a narrow vote. What does the close vote suggest?

answers.text: Most English people supported the king's right to tax without asking Parliament for approval.
Many subjects doubted the king could tax without consent, though he won.
The judges were divided over whether Parliament still existed after eleven years of silence.
Ship money had always been charged to the whole kingdom, so very few people objected to it.

questions.feedback_correct: The narrow vote showed how many people agreed with Hampden. Ship money had once been charged only to port towns, and Charles now charged it to everyone.

questions.text: In 1640 Charles called a Parliament after years of ruling without one. What forced him to do so?

answers.text: The Scots had demanded that he call it and promised to withdraw their army if he did.
Parliament had offered him a large loan in return for ending the ship money tax.
Puritans in New England had sent a petition that he could not afford to ignore any longer.
He could not pay for an army without taxes that only Parliament could grant.

questions.feedback_correct: The Scots rose against his prayer book and invaded England. Charles could not pay for an army without taxes that only Parliament could grant.

questions.text: In January 1642 Charles marched into the House of Commons with armed men to arrest five members. Why did this make war much more likely?

answers.text: No king had ever entered the Commons by force, and trust broke down.
It killed several of Parliament's leaders and left the Commons without a voice of its own.
It ended the Long Parliament and made Charles an absolute ruler of England from then on.
It caused the Scots to invade England again that spring, which began the fighting.

questions.feedback_correct: The five members had been warned and were gone, and the king's use of force shocked the Commons. Both sides began to prepare for war.

questions.text: At Putney in 1647, soldiers and officers argued over who should vote. What does this debate show about the effect of the civil war?

answers.text: The army agreed that the king should be restored to full power as soon as possible.
The Levellers and Henry Ireton agreed that every man in England should have the vote.
Once the old order cracked, people began asking who should rule and who should vote.
Parliament voted at once to give all men the vote after hearing both sides of the debate.

questions.feedback_correct: Rainsborough argued that the poorest man had a life to live as much as the greatest. Ireton replied that those without property had no lasting stake. The argument was not settled that day.

questions.text: The republic that followed the execution of Charles I did not last. Which explanation fits the lesson best?

answers.text: Charles II invaded England with a foreign army and defeated Cromwell's forces in a single battle.
It rested on Cromwell and the army, and fell apart after he died in 1658.
The Scots took over the government in 1653 and handed the crown back to the old royal family.
Parliament voted to end the republic because it had become too expensive to maintain.

questions.feedback_correct: Cromwell dissolved Parliament by force and ruled through the army. The system rested on one man, and after 1658 it fell apart. In 1660 the English invited Charles II home.

questions.text: Many Protestants put up with James II for years. Which development in 1688 did the most to change their minds?

answers.text: The death of Charles II, which left the throne open to rival claimants from several families.
The passing of the Toleration Act, which gave Catholics the right to hold public office.
The conversion of his daughter Mary to Catholicism, which split the royal family in two.
The birth of a Catholic son, who now stood ahead of his Protestant sisters.

questions.feedback_correct: Until then the crown would pass to his Protestant daughters. The birth of a son meant a Catholic dynasty, and seven leading Englishmen wrote to William of Orange.

questions.text: Parliament offered the crown to William and Mary only if they accepted the Bill of Rights. What does this show about the settlement of 1689?

answers.text: Parliament claimed power to limit the crown and even to decide who would wear it.
Parliament had abolished the monarchy and made William a servant of the Commons.
William had no legal claim to anything and was forced to leave England within a year.
James II kept the right to return to the throne if he accepted the Bill of Rights.

questions.feedback_correct: The king could no longer suspend laws, tax without consent, or keep a peacetime army without Parliament. The later Act of Settlement let Parliament choose the next ruler as well.

questions.text: France had about three times as many people as Britain, yet Britain could borrow more money and at lower cost. What best explains this?

The British king had promised to repay each loan from his own private estates and income.

questions.feedback_correct: The Bank of England and Parliament's control of taxes gave lenders confidence. French kings had been known to delay payment or cancel debts, so they paid higher interest.

questions.text: At Quebec in 1759 a single volley broke the French lines after Montcalm chose to attack at once. What does the lesson suggest about this victory?

answers.text: It owed much to a few quick choices and chances, and could have gone the other way.
It was certain from the start, because Britain had far more soldiers in Canada than France.
It ended the war, because Britain won in India and the Caribbean at the same time.
It showed that the French army was weak everywhere and could not win a battle in Europe.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson notes that a sentry who challenged the boats, or a Montcalm who waited a day, might have changed the campaign. Britain had lost battle after battle before 1759, so the outcome was not fixed in advance.

questions.text: In the Treaty of Paris, France gave up Canada but kept two small sugar islands. What does this choice suggest about how French ministers judged their colonies?

answers.text: They believed the sugar islands were easier to defend with the French navy than Canada was.
They wanted to punish the settlers of New France for refusing to pay taxes to the king.
They thought Canada was too close to the British colonies to be kept in peacetime.
They judged that the sugar islands were worth more than the snows of Canada.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson connects this to Week 21. Sugar was worth far more in trade than the fur and land of New France, which had only about 70,000 settlers.

questions.text: Why did Britain's victory in 1763 lead to a quarrel with its American colonies?

answers.text: The colonists wanted to join France after Britain took Canada from the French settlers.
The war debt had nearly doubled, so Parliament taxed colonists who had not consented.
Parliament had banned all trade between the colonies and the French sugar islands.
The king refused to send any soldiers to the frontier after the rising led by Pontiac.

questions.feedback_correct: The debt rose to about 130 million pounds, and keeping soldiers on the frontier cost more money. The Stamp Act followed in 1765, and colonists answered that they could not be taxed without their consent.

questions.text: France helped the Americans win at Yorktown in 1781. What did this victory do for France?

answers.text: It gave France Canada back and returned its Indian trading towns.
It ended the debt, because the Americans paid back the cost of the French fleet.
It brought revenge on Britain but no new land, and it added to a debt France could not easily pay.
It made Louis XVI popular enough to reform the tax system without calling anyone to approve it.

questions.feedback_correct: France spent more than a billion livres and gained no territory. Britain lost thirteen colonies but kept its credit, while the French king had no Parliament to vouch for his promises.

questions.text: Calonne proposed a land tax on every owner of land. The Assembly of Notables refused it. What does their refusal suggest?

answers.text: The nobles and officials asked to approve it would have lost their exemptions.
The Notables thought the king already had enough money and did not need new taxes.
The Notables wanted the king to call the Estates-General at once, so they voted against all taxes.
The Notables had been told by the king to refuse so that he could blame them for the debt.

questions.feedback_correct: The Notables were hand-picked from the privileged classes. A tax on every owner would have ended their exemptions.

questions.text: A hailstorm in July 1788 flattened crops across northern France. How did the failed harvest change the situation when the Estates-General met?

answers.text: It destroyed the palace at Versailles, so the king had to hold the meeting in Paris.
It persuaded the nobles to give up their exemptions so that the poor could buy bread.
It made the king dismiss Necker, whose plan for the grain trade had failed that spring.
It filled the streets with hungry, angry people and left the king less room to delay.

questions.feedback_correct: Bread prices soared, and by spring many families were hungry. The lesson says that with an ordinary harvest, reform would still have been hard but hungry crowds would not have filled the streets.

questions.text: The Estates-General met in 1789 with a dispute over voting. Why did the method of voting matter so much?

answers.text: Voting by head would have let the Third Estate, with its doubled deputies, win.
Voting by estate would have given the Third Estate two votes, one more than the clergy.
Voting by head would have forced the king to attend every session in person.
Voting by estate would have ended the privileges of the clergy and the nobles.

questions.feedback_correct: If each estate had one vote, the clergy and nobles could always outvote the Third Estate two to one. If every deputy voted as an individual, the Third Estate had as many deputies as the other two combined.

quizzes.title: 27.7 Quarterly Exam: Quarter 3: Early Modern Europe
quizzes.description: This exam covers this quarter only, covers weeks 19 to 27. It has 36 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text: Cortés founded the town of Veracruz and had its council elect him captain. Why was this a clever move?

answers.text: It gave him legal title to the Mexica capital before he had even seen the city.
It made him answer to the town and the king instead of the governor.
It freed him from paying the king's share of any gold that he might find.
It persuaded the people of the coast that Spain had already conquered them.

questions.feedback_correct: Governor Velázquez had tried to cancel the voyage. By making himself the servant of a town and the king, Cortés gave his defiance a legal cover.

questions.text: The lesson says Cortés did not have to beat the Mexica alone. What had he understood?

answers.text: The Mexica army had already been weakened by a long civil war among its leaders.
Moctezuma had promised to hand over the city if the Spaniards reached it.
Spanish steel and horses were enough to defeat any native army in the field.
Many towns hated paying tribute and would join anyone against the Mexica.

questions.feedback_correct: Cempoala and the Tlaxcalans joined him. At the final siege the Spaniards were a small part of an army with tens of thousands of native warriors.

questions.text: Why did the capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca do so much damage to the Inca state?

answers.text: All authority flowed from one man, so his generals hesitated to act.
The Inca had no roads, so no army could come to rescue him in time.
The Inca had no army and relied on their gods to defend the empire.
Atahualpa ordered his generals to surrender as soon as he was seized.

questions.feedback_correct: When the Spaniards seized Atahualpa they took the head of the whole system. His generals did not want to risk the emperor's life, and each day of hesitation helped the invaders.

questions.text: The viceroy Toledo revived the old mita at Potosí. How did the Spaniards change its purpose?

answers.text: The Inca paid it in silver coins. The Spaniards collected it in grain.
The Inca required it only in wartime. The Spaniards made it a yearly festival.
The Inca used it for roads and farms. The Spaniards used it for the mines.
The Inca forced only the rich to serve. The Spaniards made the poor serve.

questions.feedback_correct: About one worker in seven from the highland villages had to go to Potosí for a year. Cave-ins, cold, and mercury poisoning killed many.

questions.text: In 1581 the northern provinces declared that Philip II had lost the right to rule them. What reason did they give?

answers.text: He had died without leaving an heir to the throne of the Low Countries.
He had refused to learn Dutch after more than twenty years on the throne.
They said that he had broken his duties as a king toward his subjects.
He had lost the war at sea and could no longer defend their ports.

questions.feedback_correct: The northern provinces had formed the Union of Utrecht, and in 1581 they formally declared that Philip had broken the duties of a king.

questions.text: Spanish soldiers sacked Antwerp in 1576, and for a short time all seventeen provinces stood together. What happened to that unity?

answers.text: It faded, and by 1579 the mostly Catholic south made peace with Philip.
It lasted until 1648, when Spain finally accepted Dutch independence.
It ended when Philip paid his soldiers and the outrage was forgotten.
It broke when William of Orange was shot and the provinces blamed each other.

questions.feedback_correct: The outrage briefly united the provinces. It did not last: the south made peace and the north formed the Union of Utrecht.

questions.text: Why did Amsterdam grow so fast after 1585?

answers.text: The new stock exchange offered free land to anyone who would build a house there.
The Spanish king moved his court to Amsterdam to be closer to the war.
The Dutch East India Company hired thousands of sailors from the Baltic.
Spain captured Antwerp and closed its river, so merchants fled north.

questions.feedback_correct: Merchants, bankers, and skilled craftsmen fled north by the thousands. Within a few decades the city had tripled in size.

questions.text: The lesson calls Dutch toleration practical, and not equality. Which detail shows its limits?

answers.text: Jews were forbidden to build a synagogue in any Dutch city.
Only Calvinists held high office, and Catholics worshiped in secret.
Catholics held most high offices in the towns of the Republic.
Only people born in the Republic were allowed to trade in Amsterdam.

questions.feedback_correct: Jews and French Protestants were welcome, but tolerance had business sense in it and did not mean equal standing.

questions.text: The potato took a long time to win acceptance in Europe, yet it changed northern populations. Why?

answers.text: It grew well in cold, wet climates, and a small plot could feed a family.
It was cheaper to ship than wheat, so cities bought it in place of bread.
The Church urged the poor to eat it during the many fast days of the year.
It could be stored for years without spoiling, so no one starved in winter.

questions.feedback_correct: In Ireland and northern Germany populations rose. In China maize and sweet potatoes did the same on hillsides where rice would not grow.

questions.text: Why did sugar lead to large plantations rather than small farms?

answers.text: The Crown forbade small farmers to grow sugar, so only nobles could plant it.
Cane grew only on islands where no other crop would grow.
Cane needed much land, costly mills, and a great deal of labor.
Planters wanted to keep the price of sugar high by limiting the supply.

questions.feedback_correct: Cane had to be cut at the right time and crushed within a day, and the juice boiled day and night. The prize was a crop that ran on labor.

questions.text: According to the lesson, how did African states take part in the Atlantic slave trade?

answers.text: They took no part, since the Europeans seized all captives far inland.
Powerful states such as Asante and Dahomey sold captives from their wars.
They banned the trade at once and fought the Europeans along the coast.
They bought captives from Europeans and put them to work on plantations.

questions.feedback_correct: Europeans stayed near the coast, and African rulers did not allow them inland. Guns bought from Europeans made the wars that produced more captives. Not every ruler agreed, as Afonso I of Kongo showed.

questions.text: In 1781 the captain of the Zong had about 130 sick captives thrown into the sea. How did a court treat the case?

answers.text: As a murder trial, and the captain was hanged for the crime.
As a mutiny, and the sailors who refused the order were punished.
As a matter for the Admiralty, and it was never brought before a judge.
As a dispute about money, since the owners claimed insurance.

questions.feedback_correct: The court heard it as an insurance case. When the story came out in England, many people were horrified.

questions.text: In 1628 Parliament made Charles I accept the Petition of Right. What did he do next?

answers.text: He refused to sign it and sent Parliament home that same day.
He kept it faithfully for eleven years and called Parliament each spring.
He asked the judges to declare it void, and they agreed unanimously.
He agreed to it, and then he simply ignored it when it suited him.

questions.feedback_correct: The Petition said the king could not tax without consent or jail people without cause. In 1629 Charles sent Parliament home and ruled without it for eleven years.

questions.text: What was new about the New Model Army that Parliament created in 1645?

answers.text: It was paid by the king, who had agreed to share command with Parliament.
Officers were promoted for their ability and not for their birth.
It was made up of foreign soldiers hired from the Dutch Republic.
It was open only to Puritans who had sworn the Scottish Covenant.

questions.feedback_correct: The army, with Cromwell's disciplined cavalry, crushed the king at Naseby in June 1645.

questions.text: William of Orange had his own reasons to accept the invitation of 1688. What was one?

answers.text: He wanted to end the Dutch Republic by joining it to the English crown.
He had been promised a large sum of money from the English Parliament.
He wanted England as an ally against Louis XIV and not as France's friend.
He hoped to convert the English people to the Dutch Calvinist church.

questions.feedback_correct: Louis XIV threatened the Dutch Republic. William was also married to Mary, James's Protestant daughter.

questions.text: What did the Act of Settlement of 1701 show about the new English government?

answers.text: Parliament could choose the king, which no one imagined in 1600.
The king could now tax without consent so long as he called Parliament once a year.
The Church of England had taken over the power of choosing the king.
The crown would pass only to a Catholic cousin of the late king.

questions.feedback_correct: Parliament gave the crown to a Protestant German cousin, George of Hanover, who became George I in 1714.

questions.text: Why did Louis XIV make the nobles compete for places in his daily ceremonies at Versailles?

answers.text: He wanted them to learn the arts so that France would have a better army.
Only the king could grant pensions, offices, and army commands to them.
He had no other way to collect the taxes that they owed to the crown.
He wished to keep them away from the army, which was run by his ministers.

questions.feedback_correct: A noble at Versailles spent money on clothes and parties and not on a private army. The proud lords of the Fronde had become courtiers.

questions.text: The lesson says Louis XIV's rule was less absolute than it looked. Why?

answers.text: Offices were bought and inherited, and old privileges of the towns limited him.
Parliament in Paris met every year and approved each tax that he asked for.
The nobles kept private armies, so he could not give orders to the provinces.
His ministers were chosen by the great families of France, and not by the king.

questions.feedback_correct: The crown sold offices to raise money. A man who bought a judge's post could pass it to his son, and the king could do only what these groups would let him do.

questions.text: Why was the revocation of the Edict of Nantes a gift to Louis XIV's rivals?

answers.text: The Huguenots took the French navy with them and sold the ships to the Dutch.
The Huguenots led a rebellion in southern France that forced Louis to leave Paris.
Protestant kings refused to trade with France after the edict was issued.
About two hundred thousand skilled Huguenots fled to his enemies abroad.

questions.feedback_correct: The refugees included silk weavers, bankers, watchmakers, and army officers. Many Huguenot officers served William of Orange.

questions.text: The Nine Years' War is an early example of the balance of power. What does that mean?

answers.text: A strong ruler can keep peace in Europe by giving every state the same size of army.
Each state trades only with those countries that have an equal navy.
A state that grows too strong makes its neighbors unite against it.
Smaller states hand over their armies to the strongest state for protection.

questions.feedback_correct: England, the Dutch Republic, Austria, and others joined to stop Louis. The war ended in 1697 with Louis giving up many of his gains.

questions.text: Why did Newton's success give educated people a new confidence?

answers.text: It proved that the Church had been wrong about the Bible for fifteen centuries.
It gave kings the power to tax all trade between Europe and Asia.
It showed that nature followed laws that mathematics could describe.
It showed that careful observation was useless without a university degree.

questions.feedback_correct: The same force that pulled an apple to the ground held the moon in its orbit. Others soon asked whether human society might follow laws that could be found by the same patient method.

questions.text: Frederick the Great and Catherine the Great liked Enlightenment ideas. What does the lesson say about their reforms?

answers.text: They shared power with elected parliaments that wrote the new laws.
They ended monarchy in their lands and handed power to the philosophes.
They banned the Encyclopédie in their courts and burned the copies.
They reformed from above and did not give up their own power.

questions.feedback_correct: Frederick ended torture in his courts, and Catherine read the Encyclopédie. The Enlightenment could serve absolute monarchs as easily as it could challenge them.

questions.text: A ruler seizes his subjects' property and jails them without cause. Whose argument says that the people may resist him?

answers.text: Locke's, since a ruler who attacks their rights loses his claim to obey.
Montesquieu's, since only independent judges may remove a king from office.
Voltaire's, since a king is bound to follow the advice of the philosophes.
Smith's, since no government may take part in the buying and selling of goods.

questions.feedback_correct: For Locke, people set up governments by a social contract so that rulers would protect their rights to life, liberty, and property.

questions.text: What does Adam Smith's pin factory illustrate?

answers.text: The invisible hand: a king should set the price of every pin to be fair.
The division of labor: ten workers doing separate steps make thousands.
The social contract: workers agree to obey the owner who gives them wages.
The separation of powers: one worker cuts the wire and another sells the pins.

questions.feedback_correct: Ten workers who each made whole pins might make only a few hundred. Smith saw the division of labor as the secret of wealth.

questions.text: How did Frederick the Great help Britain in the Seven Years' War?

answers.text: Paid with British money, he kept French armies busy in Europe.
He sent the Prussian navy to help the British fleet attack Quebec.
He agreed to take the Ohio Valley and give Canada to Britain.
He lent Pitt a large army that sailed to India under Clive.

questions.feedback_correct: Pitt believed France could be beaten at sea and in the colonies, where it was weakest, while Frederick tied down its armies on the Continent.

questions.text: How did a trading company become a ruler in India?

answers.text: The Mughal emperor sold Bengal to the company to pay for his armies.
Clive won at Plassey, and the company took control of rich Bengal.
The French company left India and handed all its forts to the British.
Parliament sent a royal army that conquered Bengal in a single summer.

questions.feedback_correct: Clive led about 3,000 men against a far larger army. A trading firm was becoming the ruler of millions of people.

questions.text: Who bore the heaviest burden of taxation in the France of Louis XVI?

answers.text: The nobles, who paid the taille and the tithe on their own estates.
The clergy, who paid a tenth of their land to the crown each year.
The merchants, who paid the salt tax and no other tax.
Commoners and peasants, while nobles and clergy were mostly exempt.

questions.feedback_correct: Peasants paid the taille, the tithe, dues to their landlords, and a hated salt tax. A few of the wealthy held most of the exemptions.

questions.text: What did Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès argue in his pamphlet of 1789?

answers.text: That the king should give up his throne and a republic should be declared.
That the clergy and nobles should each have two votes in the Estates-General.
That the Third Estate was the whole nation and now deserved to be something.
That the Estates-General should meet every year in the city of Paris.

questions.feedback_correct: The pamphlet said that the Third Estate had been treated as nothing in politics. Most lists of complaints sent to the king were more respectful.

questions.text: What did the Assembly do on the night of August 4, 1789?

answers.text: It voted to remove the king from his throne and declared a republic.
It sold the lands of the Church and used the money to pay the army.
It gave the vote to every man and woman over the age of twenty-one.
It ended the tithe, many feudal dues, and the rights of nobles.

questions.feedback_correct: Noble after noble stood up to give up privileges. Many dues were turned into payments that peasants had to buy out, but all French people were now to stand equal before the law.

questions.text: The Declaration of the Rights of Man says that men are born free and equal. What tension does the lesson point out?

answers.text: It guarded the rights of the nobles but not those of the commoners.
It gave the king the power to veto any law that the Assembly passed.
It said "man" and meant men, and slavery continued in the colonies.
It required all citizens to belong to the Catholic Church.

questions.feedback_correct: Women could not vote, and Olympe de Gouges wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman. Protestants and Jews won full rights only after fierce debate.

questions.text: How did France raise so large an army by 1794?

answers.text: The king of Prussia lent soldiers to the Convention in return for land on the Rhine.
The levée en masse of 1793 called all French people to serve the war.
The Church paid for an army of volunteers to defend the faith.
The Vendée peasants joined the army in order to defend the Republic.

questions.feedback_correct: Within a year France had about three-quarters of a million men under arms.

questions.text: What does the lesson suggest about trying to create virtue by force?

answers.text: Virtue grows slowly through families and schools, and force may crush liberty.
Virtue can be taught in a single year if the schools are put under state control.
Force is the only way to teach virtue to a people who have lost the habit of it.
Virtue is a private matter and should have no place in the life of a republic.

questions.feedback_correct: Polybius and Machiavelli taught that republics survive on the habits of their citizens. A government that compels virtue with the guillotine may crush both virtue and liberty.

questions.text: Why were many French people glad to see Napoleon take power?

answers.text: They believed that he would restore the king and the privileges of the nobles.
They were tired of upheaval and wanted order, which he gave them.
They had voted for him in free elections that the Directory had held.
They hoped he would end all taxes and set free the prisoners of the Terror.

questions.feedback_correct: He made peace with Britain in 1802, founded the Bank of France, started the lycées, and made a Concordat with the pope.

questions.text: The Napoleonic Code kept the great gains of 1789. What else did it do?

answers.text: It restored the tithe and the special rights of the clergy.
It gave the Church the power to appoint judges in each department.
It gave husbands wide power over their wives and children.
It ended the equality of all men before the law.

questions.feedback_correct: The Code kept equality before the law, an end to feudal privilege, protection of property, and religious freedom. It was also a regime with censorship and a secret police.

questions.text: How did the Continental System lead Napoleon into Spain and Russia?

answers.text: To make the ban on British trade work, he had to control the coast of Europe.
The Spanish and Russian kings had asked him to join their war against Britain.
He wanted the silver of Spanish America to pay for the French army.
Britain had invaded both countries and Napoleon went to help them.

questions.feedback_correct: Portugal would not close its ports and was invaded in 1807. In 1812 Tsar Alexander was trading with Britain again, and Napoleon decided to punish him.

questions.text: How did Napoleon's seizure of Spain open the way for independence in Latin America?

answers.text: Napoleon sent troops to Latin America and set up colonies in each country.
The pope declared that Spanish rule in the Americas was no longer lawful.
Spain gave up its colonies in a treaty that it signed at Vienna.
With the king a prisoner, Spanish Americans asked who should rule them.

questions.feedback_correct: In 1810 councils formed in cities such as Caracas and Buenos Aires. The creoles resented Spanish-born officials, and soon some wanted more than a say.

quizzes.title: 29.5 Reading Quiz: The Nation-State
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in Week 29: The Nation-State. It has 8 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: The Congress of Vienna dealt with defeated France fairly mildly, and Talleyrand soon sat at the table as an equal. What does this suggest about the aims of the diplomats?

answers.text: They feared the French army was still strong enough to defeat all the other powers at once.
They wanted a France that was content, not one that dreamed of revenge.
They had promised Napoleon's family that France would keep every land it held in 1812.
They wanted France to pay for the Hundred Days by giving up its colonies.

questions.feedback_correct: The French kept their borders of 1792 and paid an indemnity. The statesmen believed that a harsher peace might have made France a permanent enemy.

questions.text: At Vienna the diplomats joined Belgium to the Netherlands and gave Prussia lands on the Rhine. Why did they do this?

answers.text: They wanted to punish the Belgians for supporting Napoleon during the Hundred Days.
They hoped to end the rivalry between Prussia and Austria by giving Prussia new lands in the west.
They believed the Rhine would be easy to defend, so Prussia could hold it without help.
They meant to strengthen the countries around France against a new French attack.

questions.feedback_correct: The settlement aimed at a balance of power. Stronger neighbors would make it harder for France, or anyone else, to dominate the continent again.

questions.text: Why was nationalism especially dangerous to the Austrian emperor?

answers.text: He ruled many peoples, so each one's demand for a state threatened his empire.
He had fewer soldiers than the German kings, so he could not stop nationalist risings.
He had promised at Vienna to give each people its own state within ten years.
He feared that Napoleon's nephew would use nationalism to take over Austria.

questions.feedback_correct: If each people demanded its own state, the empire could fall to pieces. That is why Metternich worked to hold the line against nationalism and liberalism.

questions.text: In 1834 Prussia led most of the German states into the Zollverein, and Austria was left out. What was the likely long-term effect?

answers.text: The German states became poorer, since fewer goods could cross their borders.
Austria became the leader of the German economy, since it did not need the union.
The German states drew closer around Prussia, opening a path to a Prussian Germany.
The German Confederation was dissolved, and every state went back to its own tariffs.

questions.feedback_correct: Goods crossed borders without tolls, merchants prospered, and railways spread. The lesson says that, without anyone intending it, a path was opening toward a Germany shaped around Prussia.

questions.text: The revolutions of 1848 spread across Europe in a few weeks and were defeated within about a year. Which explanation fits the lesson best?

answers.text: The revolutionaries had no support among the middle class, so nobody joined them.
The rulers had promised to give each country a constitution and then kept that promise.
Britain sent troops to put down the revolts in Berlin, Vienna, and Paris.
The rebels disagreed among themselves, and the old armies stayed loyal.

questions.feedback_correct: Liberals feared the workers, nationalists quarreled with other nationalists, and the Frankfurt assembly had no army of its own. Austria, with Russian help, crushed the Hungarians.

questions.text: Cavour sent Piedmontese troops to the Crimean War and later made a secret agreement with Napoleon III. What does this suggest about his judgment?

answers.text: He thought the Italian people would rise up without any help from a foreign power.
He knew that Piedmont alone could not defeat Austria and looked for an ally.
He wanted France to take over Italy and make it a French colony.
He wanted to win Garibaldi's support by showing that Piedmont could fight.

questions.feedback_correct: Cavour was a practical statesman, not a romantic. The Crimean War won Piedmont a place at the peace table, and in return for Nice and Savoy, France agreed to help drive Austria from northern Italy.

questions.text: After the Prussian victory at Königgrätz in 1866, the king and generals wanted to march on Vienna, but Bismarck argued against it. What does this show about Bismarck?

answers.text: He judged that Austria as a future friend was worth more than Austrian land.
He was afraid that Russia would enter the war if the Prussians marched on Vienna.
He wanted to keep the king from gaining too much power over the army.
He believed that Austria was too strong to be defeated in a long war.

questions.feedback_correct: Bismarck took no Austrian territory because he wanted Austria as a friend later. The lesson calls this an example of his judgment and restraint.

questions.text: What does the lesson suggest about how Italy and Germany were made?

answers.text: Great leaders were the only cause, since without Cavour and Bismarck nothing would have changed.
Deeper forces made the outcome certain, so the choices of individual leaders did not matter.
Deeper forces made unity likely, but particular decisions shaped the new states.
The great powers planned both nations at Vienna and carried out the plan in 1861 and 1871.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson says the answer is a mixture. A Germany that included Austria was entirely possible, and so was an Italy of two or three kingdoms.

quizzes.title: 32.5 Reading Quiz: The Settlement and the Dictators
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in Week 32: The Settlement and the Dictators. It has 8 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: Germans called the Treaty of Versailles a Diktat, and the French thought it too weak. According to the lesson, why was the settlement dangerous?

answers.text: It gave Germany back its colonies, which let it rebuild its navy within five years.
It forced Germany to disarm completely, so the Germans had no way to defend themselves.
It divided Germany into four zones, and each zone was run by a different victor.
It humiliated Germany but left it the strongest nation in Europe by industry.

questions.feedback_correct: Germany had not been invaded and its factories were whole. The treaty angered the Germans without taking from them the strength to try again.

questions.text: Wilson called the League of Nations the heart of the treaty, yet the League failed to stop aggression. Which explanation fits the lesson best?

answers.text: The League had its own army, but the member nations refused to allow it to fight.
It had no army, and without America the others would not act alone.
The League was dissolved in 1920, as soon as the Senate rejected the treaty.
The League lasted only until Germany joined in 1926, and then it collapsed.

questions.feedback_correct: The Senate rejected the treaty, Germany and Russia began outside the League, and the League could not force its decisions. Britain and France had been weakened by the war.

questions.text: About three million Germans found themselves in Czechoslovakia, and Hungary lost two-thirds of its land. What does this show about the peace settlement?

answers.text: Self-determination was applied unevenly, leaving millions as minorities.
The victors wanted Germany to lose land so that it could not pay for another war.
The settlement gave every national group its own state and ended all disputes over borders.
The new states had been chosen by plebiscite, so the people had accepted the new borders.

questions.feedback_correct: The principle of self-determination did not fit every case, and these grievances would return.

questions.text: In January 1918 elections gave the Bolsheviks only about a quarter of the seats in the new assembly, and Lenin dissolved it. What does this suggest about Lenin's view of the party?

answers.text: He believed that the assembly was too large to govern Russia during the civil war.
He planned to hold a second election as soon as the Whites had been defeated.
He thought a disciplined party should lead, even against the voters.
He wanted to give the soviets the right to run elections in place of the assembly.

questions.feedback_correct: Lenin held that a party of professional revolutionaries had to guide the workers. The Cheka soon hunted opponents.

questions.text: Weimar Germany seemed stable by 1925, but the Great Depression hit it especially hard. Why?

answers.text: The new government had refused all American loans and had no money to put people to work.
The republic stood on borrowed money, and American lenders called in their loans.
The Depression began in Germany, and from there it spread to the United States.
German factories had been destroyed in the war, so Germany had nothing to sell abroad.

questions.feedback_correct: Loans under the Dawes Plan had eased the burden. When the stock market crashed in 1929, the loans were called in and trade shrank, and about six million Germans were out of work.

questions.text: Stalin's Five-Year Plan built steel towns and heavy industry very fast. Who paid the main price?

answers.text: The factory workers, whose wages were cut to pay for the new machines.
The nobles, whose lands were taken and given to the soldiers who had fought for the Reds.
The Communist Party members, who were sent to the new steel towns against their will.
The peasants, whose farms were seized, and millions of whom starved in the famine.

questions.feedback_correct: Under collectivization the state seized farms and herds, and the kulaks were labeled enemies. The famine of 1932 and 1933 killed millions.

questions.text: In the March on Rome in 1922 the army could have stopped the Fascists, but the king did not call it out. What does the lesson suggest?

answers.text: The Fascists had a larger army than the Italian government, so resistance was hopeless.
Mussolini had already won a majority in parliament, so the king had no choice.
A different decision by one man might have ended Fascism that week.
The king agreed with Mussolini's plan to invade Ethiopia and wanted him in power.

questions.feedback_correct: King Victor Emmanuel III asked Mussolini to form a government. The lesson says that a different decision by one man might have ended Fascism that week.

questions.text: Hitler became chancellor in January 1933. Which description fits the lesson?

answers.text: It was legal but not inevitable, since conservatives hoped to control him.
It was a violent coup, in which Nazi troops seized the capital and forced Hindenburg to resign.
It was certain from 1928, when the Nazis won a majority of the votes in a national election.
It was the result of a popular vote in which Hitler won more than half of all voters.

questions.feedback_correct: The Nazis won thirty-seven percent in July 1932, never a majority. Papen and others pressed Hindenburg to name Hitler, and a different decision by a few men might have kept him out.

quizzes.title: 34.5 Reading Quiz: The Cold War and Communism
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in Week 34: The Cold War and Communism. It has 8 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: At Yalta, Stalin agreed to free elections in Eastern Europe, but by 1946 Soviet-backed communists were taking power there. What best explains his actions?

answers.text: He believed that the Western powers had already broken the agreement by dividing Germany.
He had never seen the text of the agreement and learned of it only after the Red Army left.

He wanted the satellite states to accept American money to rebuild after the war.

questions.text: Why did Secretary of State Marshall propose to help rebuild Western Europe?

answers.text: Poverty fed communist parties, and recovery would weaken their appeal.
Britain had asked America to take over its colonies and needed money to defend them.
The satellite states had asked for American loans, and Stalin had agreed to allow them.
The United Nations had ordered the richest nations to pay for Europe's rebuilding.

questions.feedback_correct: Western Europe lay in ruins, and communist parties were strong in France and Italy. Stalin refused the aid for his own sphere and forced the satellite states to refuse as well.

questions.text: When Stalin blockaded West Berlin, Truman refused to give way but did not want a ground war. What does the Berlin Airlift show?

answers.text: The Western powers had given up West Berlin and were helping people to leave.
The blockade had failed because Soviet troops let the trucks through at night.
The Americans and British had planned to attack East Germany by air if the blockade continued.
It was a way to resist the blockade without starting a war on the ground.

questions.feedback_correct: Planes landed every few minutes for nearly a year, bringing coal, food, and medicine to two million people. Stalin ended the blockade in May 1949.

questions.text: The lesson tells of a Soviet submarine near Cuba in 1962 where one officer refused to agree to launch a nuclear torpedo. What does the story suggest?

answers.text: The Soviet navy had ordered its submarines to attack American ships on sight.
The danger was greater than leaders knew, and much rested on individual judgment.
The American ships had agreed to leave the area as soon as they spotted the submarine.
The crisis was never close to war, since the officers on the submarine had no real power.

questions.feedback_correct: The decision required agreement from three officers, and Vasili Arkhipov refused. Whether or not the story is exactly right, it shows how much rested on individual judgment.

questions.text: Factories in the Soviet Union met their quotas by making goods nobody needed, and shops had long lines and empty shelves. What does this suggest about a command economy?

answers.text: Planners had no price signals, and workers had little reward for good work.
Soviet workers were lazier than workers in other countries and did not wish to produce more.
The government had ordered the factories to make too few goods so that prices would stay high.
The planners had made too many mistakes in arithmetic when they set the targets.

questions.feedback_correct: Planners could not know what millions of people wanted. Without the chance to profit, there was little reward for new ideas, and leaders were often told what they wished to hear.

questions.text: The Great Leap Forward led to the worst famine in history. Which cause does the lesson give?

answers.text: Mao ordered the army to take the harvest from the peasants to feed the cities.
The Soviet Union cut off all grain to China after the two countries quarreled.
Harvests were neglected and officials reported false numbers to please superiors.
A severe drought lasted three years, and the government refused foreign help.

questions.feedback_correct: Peasants were forced into huge communes and made steel in backyard furnaces. Because officials reported false numbers, the leaders did not know how bad things were.

questions.text: Gorbachev told the leaders of the satellite states that the Soviet Union would no longer send in tanks. The lesson calls this the decisive choice. Why?

answers.text: It allowed the Soviet Union to move its troops home and spend the money on the economy.
With the fear of Soviet tanks gone, the system began to unravel.
It made the leaders of the satellite states resign at once, so that elections could be held.
It meant that Gorbachev had given up on reform and was planning to retire.

questions.feedback_correct: Gorbachev expected reformed communism to survive. Instead, once the old fear was gone, communist governments fell in Poland, Hungary, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, and Romania.

questions.text: On November 9, 1989, East German guards gave way when crowds rushed to the Berlin Wall. What does this suggest about the East German government?

answers.text: The guards had received an order from Moscow to open the gates in the Wall.
The government had planned for years to open the Wall and had told the guards to wait.
The crowd was armed and forced the guards to leave their posts.
A government that would have shot people in 1961 now had no will to do so.

questions.feedback_correct: An official had announced, confused about the rules, that new travel rules took effect immediately. The guards, without orders, gave way.
