quizzes.title: 36.7 Quarterly Exam: Quarter 4: Late Modernity
quizzes.description: This exam covers this quarter only, covers weeks 28 to 36. It has 36 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text: Why did industrialization begin in Britain and not somewhere else?

answers.text: Britain had more people than any other country, so it had more workers for its mills.
The Crown ordered the building of the first factories and paid for each of them.
Cheap coal and fairly high wages made machines that saved labor a good bargain.
Britain had banned the export of cotton, so its mills had no foreign rivals.

questions.feedback_correct: Coal lay close to the surface and the sea. Settled government, canals, savings, and skilled craftsmen did the rest. Nobody planned it, and none of it made the outcome certain.

questions.text: How did Watt's improved steam engine change where factories could be built?

answers.text: It could turn a wheel, so a factory no longer had to sit beside a fast river.
It could run on wood alone, so factories could be built far from the coal mines.
It was small enough to be built into each worker's cottage.
It made the water wheel faster, so more factories were built on rivers.

questions.feedback_correct: Watt's separate condenser used far less coal. After Watt and Boulton became partners in 1775, a factory could stand anywhere a cart of coal could reach.

questions.text: What did the Factory Act of 1833 do that earlier appeals had not?

answers.text: It banned all work by women and children in every kind of factory.
It set a ten-hour day for every worker in every trade.
It gave the workers the right to vote in the next election.
It created paid inspectors to see that the law was kept.

questions.feedback_correct: It barred children under nine from textile mills and limited the hours of older children. The Ten Hours Act of 1847 came later.

questions.text: Marx expected the workers of the most industrial country to rebel first. What happened in Britain?

answers.text: The workers rose in 1848 and the army put down the revolt in a few days.
Wages rose, unions grew, and Parliament widened the vote for workers.
The mill owners gave their factories to the workers and left the country.
Parliament banned all unions and the workers were too afraid to protest.

questions.feedback_correct: The revolutions that later took Marx's name broke out in Russia, a farming country.

questions.text: What did the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 do?

answers.text: They gave each German state a written constitution and an elected assembly.
They put universities under watch, banned student clubs, and censored books.
They joined Austria and Prussia into a single country under one emperor.
They freed the peasants of Prussia from the dues that they owed to the nobles.

questions.feedback_correct: Metternich used the murder of Kotzebue to push them through the German Confederation. Spies and police were common.

questions.text: Why did the Frankfurt assembly of 1848 fail to unite Germany?

answers.text: The Austrian army occupied Frankfurt on the first day of the meeting.
The assembly voted to unite with France and the Germans refused to follow.
The assembly could not agree on a language for the new constitution.
The Prussian king refused its crown, and it had no army to back it.

questions.feedback_correct: Frederick William IV would not take a crown from an assembly of commoners or break with the German princes. The assembly was scattered in 1849.

questions.text: How did Garibaldi help to unite Italy?

answers.text: He took the south with volunteers and gave it to the king.
He defeated the Austrians at Solferino and took Venetia for Piedmont.
He persuaded the pope to give up Rome and join the new kingdom.
He led the army of Piedmont in the war of 1859 and signed the peace.

questions.feedback_correct: In May 1860 he landed in Sicily with volunteers in red shirts. He then met Victor Emmanuel II, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861.

questions.text: How did Bismarck use the telegram from Ems in 1870?

answers.text: He kept it secret so that France would be taken by surprise.
He sent it to the Austrians to persuade them to join Prussia.
He edited it to sound sharper, and France declared war.
He published it unchanged to prove that the French had insulted the king.

questions.feedback_correct: The southern German states then joined Prussia. William was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles in January 1871.

questions.text: Which developments helped Europeans conquer so much of Africa after 1870?

answers.text: Railways that crossed the whole of Africa before 1850 and cheap iron ships.
Alliances with every African ruler and the consent of the Berlin conference.
Large European armies that landed in Africa and stayed for several years.
Steamships, the telegraph, quinine, and the Maxim gun gave them an edge.

questions.feedback_correct: The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and shortened voyages. Quinine protected Europeans against malaria, and breech-loading rifles gave small forces great firepower.

questions.text: Why did Ethiopia keep its independence when most of Africa did not?

answers.text: Britain and France agreed at Berlin that Ethiopia should be left alone.
Menelik II bought modern rifles, trained his army, and won at Adwa.
Ethiopia had no valuable land, and the Europeans were not interested.
The emperor signed a treaty that made Ethiopia a protectorate of Italy.

questions.feedback_correct: Ethiopia and Liberia were the only African lands to keep their independence.

questions.text: What led to the First Opium War?

answers.text: The Qianlong Emperor refused Macartney's request for freer trade in 1793.
The Taiping rebels attacked the British ships at Shanghai.
Lin Zexu destroyed British opium, and merchants demanded payment.
Britain wanted to stop the sale of opium in China, and China refused.

questions.feedback_correct: Lin seized and destroyed more than twenty thousand chests in 1839. Some in Parliament thought the war a disgrace, but a fleet was sent.

questions.text: What did the samurai of Satsuma and Choshu learn from the Western bombardments of 1863 and 1864?

answers.text: Swords could not expel foreigners; they had to learn Western ways.
The shogun was strong enough to defeat the Western ships without their help.
Japan should sign treaties with every nation and give up its own army.
The emperor should give up his throne and move to the city of Edo.

questions.feedback_correct: In January 1868 these samurai seized the palace in Kyoto and declared the emperor restored to power.

questions.text: How did the Schlieffen Plan make war more likely in 1914?

answers.text: It called for a quick blow at France before Russia could mobilize.
It required Germany to wait for an attack by France before it could mobilize.
It promised Britain that Germany would respect the neutrality of Belgium.
It asked Austria to attack Russia first and then take the Balkans.

questions.feedback_correct: All the plans depended on speed, and each country's mobilization looked like an act of war to its neighbors.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call the death of Franz Ferdinand ironic?

answers.text: He was killed by an assassin sent by his own government.
He had ordered the driver to turn right on that street.
He had often argued against going to war with Serbia.
He had planned to give Bosnia to Serbia within a year.

questions.feedback_correct: Princip stepped forward because the driver took a wrong turn and stopped to back up in front of a delicatessen.

questions.text: Why did attacks on the Western Front so often fail?

answers.text: Both armies lacked shells, and they could not keep up their bombardments.
Machine guns and artillery gave the defenders a decisive advantage.
The armies were too small to man a line that ran from the Channel to Switzerland.
The generals ordered every attack to begin in daylight, and soldiers refused.

questions.feedback_correct: On the first day of the Somme, nearly sixty thousand British soldiers were killed or wounded. By November the line had moved only a few miles.

questions.text: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in January 1917. What did this help to bring about?

answers.text: The end of the British blockade of Germany and the return of food.
The surrender of Russia and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.
The collapse of Austria-Hungary and the end of the Habsburg throne.
The entry of the United States into the war on the Allied side.

questions.feedback_correct: Congress declared war on April 6, 1917. Soon more than a million American soldiers were in France.

questions.text: Why did Clemenceau want a harsh peace?

answers.text: He believed Germany had been punished enough and wanted to move on quickly.
He wanted Germany to join the League of Nations as soon as possible.
France had lost over a million men and was invaded twice in fifty years.
He had promised Wilson that France would take no land from Germany.

questions.feedback_correct: Wilson had hoped for self-determination and a League. Lloyd George feared pushing Germany too hard.

questions.text: How did the Bolsheviks win the civil war against the Whites?

answers.text: Britain, France, Japan, and the United States sent large armies to help the Reds.
The Reds had many more soldiers than the Whites in every battle.
The Whites were driven out when Lenin gave land to the nobles.
The Whites were divided, and the Reds held the cities and railways.

questions.feedback_correct: The war lasted until 1921 and famine and fighting killed millions. Foreign troops came at various times, but not enough to matter.

questions.text: What caused the German hyperinflation of 1923?

answers.text: France occupied the Ruhr and the government printed money.
The Dawes Plan ended all American loans to Germany in 1923.
The stock market in New York crashed and the banks in Germany failed.
The Kaiser returned and ordered the treasury to pay his old soldiers.

questions.feedback_correct: The government printed money to pay striking workers, and the savings of the middle class vanished.

questions.text: What did Stalin, Mussolini, and Hitler have in common, despite their differences?

answers.text: Each came to power by winning more than half of the votes in free elections.
One party, one leader, a secret police, and an enemy within.
Each was supported by the Church and by the old nobility.
Each ruled through an elected parliament that had real power over taxes.

questions.feedback_correct: They took advantage of fear, humiliation, and economic ruin. In each case particular decisions by other people also mattered.

questions.text: What did the Munich agreement of 1938 cost Czechoslovakia?

answers.text: Its alliance with France, which was ended at once by the French parliament.
Its mountain defenses, and in 1939 the rest of the country.
Its army, which was disbanded by order of the four powers.
Its government, which was moved to London during the war.

questions.feedback_correct: This broke Hitler's promise and showed that his aims went beyond Germans living outside Germany.

questions.text: How were the Germans able to defeat France in about six weeks in 1940?

answers.text: Tanks crossed the Ardennes, which the French thought impassable.
They broke through the Maginot Line with heavy artillery in a single week.
They had many more tanks and planes than France and Britain combined.
They landed from the sea in Normandy and took Paris by surprise.

questions.feedback_correct: The tanks reached the Channel in ten days and trapped the British and some French forces at Dunkirk.

questions.text: How did Nazi persecution of the Jews move through stages?

answers.text: From a boycott of shops to a ban on travel, and then expulsion of all Jews to Palestine.
From a ban on marriage to a boycott, and then to a peace treaty at Wannsee.
From removing rights to violence, ghettos, shootings, and killing centers.
From laws to violence, and then to a vote by the Reichstag to end the war.

questions.feedback_correct: The Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht, the ghettos, the Einsatzgruppen, and the killing centers were successive steps. The Final Solution was coordinated at Wannsee in January 1942.

questions.text: A crime of this size needed many hands. What does the lesson say about the people who took part?

answers.text: Nearly all of them were party members who had been ordered to take part.
Nearly all refused to obey, and the plan was carried out by a few.
Nearly all were foreigners brought in from the occupied lands.
Many were not fanatics, though some resisted and rescuers were rare.

questions.feedback_correct: Clerks, police, soldiers, doctors, and engineers played a part. Some, such as the villagers of Le Chambon and the Danes, resisted.

questions.text: What did the Truman Doctrine mark?

answers.text: The end of the Marshall Plan and the withdrawal of American troops from Germany.
A pledge that the United States would never use atomic weapons first.
An alliance of Britain, France, and the Soviet Union to defend Greece.
The United States took on lasting peacetime commitments in Europe.

questions.feedback_correct: Britain could no longer support Greece and Turkey in 1947. Truman asked Congress for aid to free peoples resisting pressure.

questions.text: Why did the nuclear arms race help to keep peace in Europe?

answers.text: Neither side could attack without being destroyed in return.
Both sides agreed to give up their atomic bombs after the Berlin Airlift.
The United Nations took control of all the weapons in 1949.
Only the United States had hydrogen bombs, and no one dared to challenge it.

questions.feedback_correct: This was deterrence, sometimes called mutual assured destruction. The contest still spread to other parts of the world, as in Korea.

questions.text: How did events in Poland help to crack the Soviet bloc?

answers.text: The Polish army overthrew the government and left the Warsaw Pact in 1980.
The Soviet Union gave Poland its freedom in return for coal and grain.
The pope's visit and Solidarity showed Poles they were not alone.
The Polish government welcomed Solidarity and made it the ruling party.

questions.feedback_correct: Martial law in 1981 jailed Solidarity's leaders, but could not kill the movement. In 1989 Solidarity won nearly every seat it was allowed to contest.

questions.text: What did Deng Xiaoping change in China, and what did he keep?

answers.text: He ended the party's rule and held free elections in 1989.
He let people work for profit, but the party kept power.
He closed the schools and sent the young to the countryside.
He ended the economy of the commune and restored the landlords.

questions.feedback_correct: China's economy began to grow quickly. In June 1989 the party crushed the protests in Tiananmen Square.

questions.text: Why did Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance work against Britain?

answers.text: It depended on an opponent who could be shamed by seeing suffering.
It relied on the British army being too small to arrest the protesters.
It was backed by the Muslim League and by the armies of the princes.
It brought immediate help from the United Nations and the Soviet Union.

questions.feedback_correct: The British had a free press and a conscience. Historians note that the same tactics would have met a different fate against a regime like Stalin's or Hitler's.

questions.text: What made the partition of India in 1947 so violent?

answers.text: Britain left India in 1950, and the new states had no time to prepare.
The Indian army refused to guard the new border, and so did the police.
The princes refused to join either India or Pakistan, and they went to war.
A lawyer who had never seen India drew the border in a few weeks.

questions.feedback_correct: Perhaps ten to fifteen million people crossed the new lines, and mobs on all sides killed their neighbors. Mountbatten had set the date earlier than expected.

questions.text: Why did Britain's wartime promises about the Middle East cause so much trouble later?

answers.text: It promised Palestine to the Ottomans and then took it by force.
It made promises to Arabs, to France, and to Zionist leaders.
It promised Egypt independence and then closed the Suez Canal.
It promised all its lands to the League of Nations after the war.

questions.feedback_correct: Hussein of Mecca, the Sykes-Picot Agreement, and the Balfour Declaration could not all be kept.

questions.text: The lesson says that each side tells the story of 1948 differently. How?

answers.text: Palestinians call it a victory, and Israelis call it a defeat.
Both sides call it a civil war, and neither side blames the other.
Palestinians call it the Nakba, and Israelis call it independence.
Israelis call it the Nakba, and Palestinians call it a War of Independence.

questions.feedback_correct: About seven hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs left or were driven from their homes, and historians continue to debate how many of each.

questions.text: How did the Shah lose his throne in 1979?

answers.text: The army overthrew him and gave power to Khomeini in a single night.
The United States removed him in a plan to put Mossadegh back in power.
Strikes and protests grew after soldiers fired, and the Shah left Iran.
The Iraqi army invaded Iran and the Shah was killed in the fighting.

questions.feedback_correct: The Shah was secretly ill with cancer, and some of his generals lost heart. A different response in 1978 might have kept him on the throne.

questions.text: How did the war in Afghanistan help to give rise to al-Qaeda?

answers.text: The Soviets trained bin Laden, who later turned against them.
Volunteers joined the fight, and bin Laden helped to fund them.
The Taliban built al-Qaeda to defend Afghanistan against the United States.
The United States asked bin Laden to attack its own embassies in Africa.

questions.feedback_correct: After the Soviets left in 1989 the world lost interest, and the Taliban later gave bin Laden a base.

questions.text: What did Robert Schuman propose in 1950?

answers.text: To form a single European army under French and German command.
To make Germany pay reparations in coal and steel to France.
To end all tariffs between the nations of Europe at once.
To put French and German coal and steel under one authority.

questions.feedback_correct: Coal and steel were the stuff of weapons, so such a pact would make war between the two materially impossible. Six nations formed the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951.

questions.text: What does the lesson conclude about the internet and other tools of globalization?

answers.text: They carry both effects, because people, and not tools, decide how they are used.
They are good for the world, and any harm comes from governments that misuse them.
They are harmful to the world, and every nation should limit their use.
They are neutral and have little effect on how people live and think.

questions.feedback_correct: The same network lets a student read the same books as one in a great city, and lets a hidden network spread a lie as quickly as a doctor can share a cure.

quizzes.title: 36.8 Semester Final Exam: Weeks 19 to 36
quizzes.description: This exam covers the whole semester, Weeks 19 to 36. It has 50 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text: The lesson doubts the story that Moctezuma took Cortés for a returning god. What is the main reason?

answers.text: The story comes mostly from sources written after the conquest.
Moctezuma never met Cortés before the Spaniards entered the city.
The Mexica had no gods who were said to return from the east.
Cortés wrote that Moctezuma had refused to speak with him at all.

questions.feedback_correct: A simpler explanation is more likely: Moctezuma was curious, cautious, and unsure what the strangers wanted.

questions.text: How did the civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa help Pizarro?

answers.text: Huáscar sent his own army to join the Spaniards against his brother.
The Inca had given up their roads and left the mountains undefended.
The armies were worn out, and the best generals had been lost.
Atahualpa had already agreed to pay tribute to the king of Spain.

questions.feedback_correct: Pizarro arrived as the war ended. A year earlier he would have met a united empire.

questions.text: Why could even the silver of Peru and Mexico not solve Philip II's money troubles?

answers.text: The silver ships were seized by Dutch pirates before they reached Spain.
The Crown gave all of the silver to the Church, which spent it on buildings.
The silver lost its value when the Dutch began to make coins from tin.
He fought the Turks and the Dutch rebels, and the bills were too large.

questions.feedback_correct: His government went bankrupt in 1575, and his unpaid soldiers mutinied.

questions.text: What did the Dutch East India Company do in the Banda Islands in 1621?

answers.text: It signed a treaty that let the islanders sell nutmeg to any buyer they chose.
It killed or enslaved most islanders to enforce its nutmeg monopoly.
It gave the islands to the Dutch government in return for a large payment.
It built a port at Batavia and left the islanders to govern themselves.

questions.feedback_correct: The islanders had refused to sell only to the Dutch. The monopoly was enforced by arms as well as by contract.

questions.text: What happened to the Taíno after Columbus arrived in the Caribbean?

answers.text: They moved to the mainland and built new towns in the mountains of Peru.
They joined the Spaniards and grew rich on the plantations of Hispaniola.
They nearly vanished in two generations, from disease and forced labor.
They were protected by the Spanish king, and their numbers grew steadily.

questions.feedback_correct: The Spaniards did not understand what was happening, and they did not intend it.

questions.text: What does the letter of Afonso I of Kongo to the king of Portugal show?

answers.text: The slave trade was criticized from the start, including by African rulers.
The kings of Kongo were the largest sellers of captives on the West African coast.
The king of Portugal had agreed to stop the trade after his complaint.
Christian kings in Africa had no way to communicate with Europe.

questions.feedback_correct: Afonso wrote in 1526 that Portuguese merchants were kidnapping his people. The king of Portugal never stopped the trade.

questions.text: What did Puritan emigration in the 1630s do to England and to America?

answers.text: It ended the quarrel between Charles and Parliament over taxes.
It drained England of reformers and gave America Puritan roots.
It made the Puritans a small group with no voice in the Civil War.
It filled the new colonies with Catholics who had fled from Laud.

questions.feedback_correct: Thousands sailed across the Atlantic and founded colonies such as Massachusetts Bay.

questions.text: Why did the trial of the seven bishops in 1688 turn so many English people against James II?

answers.text: The bishops were found guilty of treason and the king had them executed.
The king proved that Parliament had no right to oppose him in court.
The jury was made up of Catholics who voted in favor of the bishops.
Many feared a king of divine right who might rule without Parliament.

questions.feedback_correct: A jury found the bishops not guilty, and London rang with celebration.

questions.text: Why did Louis XIV rely on intendants in the provinces?

answers.text: They were great nobles who had sworn an oath to defend the Church.
They were generals who commanded the armies of each province.
They were elected by the towns and answered to the local judges.
They were officials from lawyers and townsmen with no local power.

questions.feedback_correct: Because they had no local base, they depended on the king. They collected taxes, kept order, and recruited soldiers.

questions.text: What tax reform did Marshal Vauban propose, and how did Louis respond?

answers.text: A tax on all foreign trade. Louis accepted it and named Vauban a minister.
A fairer tax that nobles and clergy would also pay. Louis banned the book.
A tax on Versailles itself. Louis agreed and sold part of the palace.
A tax on the Church only. Louis rejected it because the pope objected.

questions.feedback_correct: Vauban died soon after. His plan went unused, and the problem he named stayed with France for the rest of the century.

questions.text: What was the Republic of Letters?

answers.text: A network of scholars across Europe who wrote in Latin and French.
A court in Paris that tried writers who published without the king's leave.
A group of kings who agreed to share the cost of printing the Encyclopédie.
A school in London where the sons of nobles were taught to read.

questions.feedback_correct: Learned societies such as the Royal Society in London and the Academy of Sciences in Paris helped. Cheaper printing did the rest.

questions.text: What cause did Voltaire take up in the case of Jean Calas?

answers.text: Free trade. He wrote a pamphlet against the tax on salt.
The social contract. He asked the king to give the people a constitution.
Toleration. He campaigned for three years to overturn the verdict.
The separation of powers. He wrote a book to praise the English judges.

questions.feedback_correct: Calas, a Protestant merchant, was executed in Toulouse on a false charge in 1762.

questions.text: Why did the Proclamation of 1763 anger many American colonists?

answers.text: It ordered them to pay for the French and Indian War out of their own savings.
It forbade settlement beyond the Appalachians, where many hoped to claim land.
It required every colonist to swear loyalty to the Church of England.
It taxed every colonist who wished to buy or sell goods in the thirteen colonies.

questions.feedback_correct: London meant to keep order on the frontier after Pontiac's rising, but keeping soldiers there cost money.

questions.text: A parlement in France could refuse to register a royal law. How did it differ from the British Parliament?

answers.text: It was an assembly of the clergy that met in the king's palace.
It was a council of the king's ministers that could not refuse his orders.
It was a group of generals that decided how taxes would be spent.
It was a high law court and not an elected assembly of the people.

questions.feedback_correct: In 1788 the parlement of Paris said that only the Estates-General could approve the new taxes.

questions.text: Why did the flight to Varennes damage the Constitution of 1791?

answers.text: The king had taken the army with him and had declared war on France.
The Assembly learned that the king had signed a treaty with the pope.
Most people believed the king had tried to desert the Revolution.
The royal family had reached the frontier and left France for good.

questions.feedback_correct: A constitution that depended on the king's honest cooperation lost its foundation. The family was brought back from Varennes.

questions.text: What happened on the ninth of Thermidor?

answers.text: Deputies shouted Robespierre down, and he was executed the next day.
Robespierre dissolved the Convention and made himself the ruler of France.
The army marched on Paris and put the Committee of Public Safety on trial.
The Paris city government freed Robespierre and put the Convention to flight.

questions.feedback_correct: The Terror ended, though not at once. Prisoners were freed, the Jacobin club was closed, and the Directory took power in 1795.

questions.text: What saved Napoleon at Saint-Cloud during the coup of Brumaire?

answers.text: The army of the Directory refused to fire on its own commander.
The deputies voted to give him power after hearing his speech.
Lucien told the soldiers the deputies had tried to stab Napoleon.
Sieyès arrested the leaders of the councils before they could act.

questions.feedback_correct: The troops cleared the hall. The lesson says a few steadier nerves in the hall might have left Napoleon an exile or a prisoner.

questions.text: How did yellow fever change the map of the Americas around 1803?

answers.text: It killed Toussaint Louverture, and Haiti became a French colony again.
It killed most French soldiers in Haiti, and Napoleon sold Louisiana.
It spread among the Spanish troops and let Bolívar free Venezuela.
It ended the war between France and Britain, and Louisiana was left to Spain.

questions.feedback_correct: Haiti declared its independence in 1804. A disease had changed the map.

questions.text: What bottleneck did inventors such as Hargreaves and Arkwright attack in the making of cloth?

answers.text: One spinner made one thread at a time, so weavers waited for yarn.
Cotton was too expensive to import, so mills lacked raw material.
Looms could not be powered by water, so weaving was done by hand.
Dyes were scarce, so cloth could not be sold outside Britain.

questions.feedback_correct: The spinning jenny, the water frame, the mule, and the power loom each answered a part of the problem.

questions.text: What did Robert Owen's mills at New Lanark show?

answers.text: A mill could not make a profit unless it hired children.
Workers would not accept good schools and fair prices.
A model village could succeed only in the United States.
A mill could be run with decency and still make a profit.

questions.feedback_correct: He cut the working day, refused to hire young children, built a school, and cleaned up the village. His later community at New Harmony broke up within a few years.

questions.text: What was the Concert of Europe?

answers.text: An agreement among the great powers to meet when trouble arose.
A treaty among Germany's states to make war against France together.
A pledge by the Christian kings to defend the pope in Rome.
A union of the Italian states under the king of Piedmont.

questions.feedback_correct: The Congress of Vienna was judged by the first test of any regime, which was whether it kept the peace. No great war engulfed Europe until 1854.

questions.text: Why did Napoleon III sign a sudden peace with Austria in 1859?

answers.text: He had been defeated at Solferino and could not continue the war.
He had received Venetia and Lombardy from Austria in return.
He had been asked by the pope to protect Rome from Piedmont.
He was alarmed by the cost and by the nationalism he had set loose.

questions.feedback_correct: Venetia remained in Austrian hands, and Cavour resigned in anger.

questions.text: What happened to the East India Company after the revolt of 1857?

answers.text: It was given the right to raise its own army from the Punjab.
It moved its capital from Calcutta to Delhi.
Parliament abolished it and put India directly under the Crown.
It was sold to the princes who had stayed loyal to Britain.

questions.feedback_correct: This was the Raj. In 1877 Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India.

questions.text: What did the treaties of 1854 and 1858 do to Japan?

answers.text: They closed the ports of Japan to all Western ships for another century.
They opened ports to American trade on terms like those forced on China.
They gave Hokkaido to the United States as a naval base.
They made the emperor of Japan a servant of the American president.

questions.feedback_correct: The shogun's advisers were divided, and they knew the Chinese had already lost to the British.

questions.text: Why did Bismarck's alliance system come apart after 1890?

answers.text: It was ended by a vote of the German parliament in 1890.
It rested on one man, whom Wilhelm II dismissed in 1890.
It was undone when Italy joined the Triple Entente in 1894.
It collapsed when Britain declared war on Germany in 1890.

questions.feedback_correct: Russia and France then signed an alliance in 1894, and Germany had enemies on both sides.

questions.text: What did the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk do?

answers.text: It ended the war in the west and sent American troops home.
It made Russia a member of the Triple Entente again.
It gave Germany much Russian land and freed its armies.
It gave Poland to Austria and Finland to Germany.

questions.feedback_correct: Freed from the east, Germany tried a great offensive in the spring of 1918.

questions.text: What did Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles say?

answers.text: Germany must give up its colonies and its navy.
Germany would join the League of Nations at once.
Germany must return Alsace and Lorraine within a year.
Germany and its allies were responsible for the war.

questions.feedback_correct: On that basis Germany owed reparations, which a commission set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks.

questions.text: What did Stalin's Great Purge do to the Communist Party?

answers.text: Show trials forced old Bolsheviks to confess, and many were shot.
It made the party larger by letting in workers and peasants.
It gave Trotsky the leadership of the party after Lenin.
It ended the Five-Year Plan and returned the land to the peasants.

questions.feedback_correct: Millions more went to the labor camps of the Gulag.

questions.text: Why was the surrender at Stalingrad a turning point?

answers.text: The United States entered the war after the Germans sank an American ship.
Hitler agreed to retreat and the Germans withdrew from Russia.
The Japanese attacked Siberia, and the Soviets made peace with Hitler.
A German army of 200,000 was lost, and the Soviets began to advance.

questions.feedback_correct: Hitler had forbidden retreat. The army surrendered in February 1943.

questions.text: What did the Nuremberg court hold about orders from a superior?

answers.text: That obedience to orders was no defense for such crimes.
That a soldier who obeyed an order could never be tried.
That only the Führer could be held to account for the war.
That orders given in wartime were outside the law.

questions.feedback_correct: Twelve defendants were sentenced to death. The word genocide had been coined by Raphael Lemkin in 1944.

questions.text: What was the pledge of NATO in 1949?

answers.text: Members would share their atomic weapons with the Soviet Union.
An attack on one member was an attack on all.
Members would lend money to rebuild the countries of Eastern Europe.
Members would keep their armies out of Germany.

questions.feedback_correct: The Soviets formed the Warsaw Pact in 1955 with their satellites.

questions.text: What did the Brezhnev Doctrine declare?

answers.text: The Soviets would let each satellite state choose its own government.
The Soviets would reduce their armies if the West did the same.
The Soviets would act if socialism was threatened in a member state.
The Soviets would open the borders of Eastern Europe to trade.

questions.feedback_correct: Brezhnev sent Warsaw Pact troops into Czechoslovakia in 1968 after the Prague Spring.

questions.text: What did the Suez affair of 1956 show about Britain and France?

answers.text: They had won back control of the canal by their own power.
They could no longer act as great powers on their own.
They had forced the United States to side with them.
They had the full support of the Soviet Union.

questions.feedback_correct: The United States and the Soviet Union both demanded that they stop, and they withdrew.

questions.text: What did the Oslo Accords of 1993 create?

answers.text: A fully independent Palestinian state with its capital in Jerusalem.
A final peace treaty that settled all the borders of Israel.
A United Nations force to guard the holy places of Jerusalem.
A Palestinian Authority to govern parts of the West Bank and Gaza.

questions.feedback_correct: The hardest questions, such as borders, Jerusalem, refugees, and settlements, were left unsettled.

questions.text: Why did many Iranians resent the United States by 1979?

answers.text: It had sold weapons to Iraq before the war with Iran began.
It had invaded Iran to protect the oil fields in 1951.
It had helped remove Mossadegh in 1953 and backed the Shah.
It had made the Shah give up his throne in favor of Khomeini.

questions.feedback_correct: The Shah's alliance with America made the United States a target of anger.

questions.text: How did the shipping container lower the cost of trade?

answers.text: A crate could go from ship to train to truck without opening.
It let ships sail faster by carrying fewer goods on each voyage.
It let customs officers inspect every crate at a single port.
It let goods be sold before they were made in the factories.

questions.feedback_correct: Loading costs dropped sharply, and it became cheap to make goods far from where they were sold.

questions.text: Several lessons describe a small event that might have changed history, such as the Quebec cliff path, the hall at Saint-Cloud, and the wrong turn at Sarajevo. What does the course suggest?

answers.text: Great events always had one cause, and small events did not matter.
Historians can tell in advance which events will change the world.
Outcomes depended on particular choices and chances, not on fate.
Leaders had little power, since large forces decided everything.

questions.feedback_correct: The lessons repeatedly ask what would have happened if one person had chosen differently.

questions.text: Britain borrowed cheaply, the Dutch built a bourse, and the French kings paid higher interest. What do the lessons suggest about credit?

answers.text: States whose lenders trusted a parliament could borrow more cheaply.
States with the largest populations could always borrow the most.
States with a king could borrow more cheaply because he was always repaid.
States that held the most silver had no need to borrow at all.

questions.feedback_correct: Lenders trusted Parliament more than a king, and French kings had been known to delay or cancel debts.

questions.text: The Dutch tolerated several faiths, while Louis XIV drove out the Huguenots. What did each choice bring?

answers.text: The Dutch lost many skilled people, and Louis gained a united kingdom.
Both kingdoms grew richer, and both avoided war with their neighbors.
Neither choice had any effect on trade or on the strength of the state.
The Dutch gained skilled people, and Louis armed his rivals with them.

questions.feedback_correct: Tolerance in Amsterdam had good business sense in it. The Huguenots who fled included weavers, bankers, and army officers.

questions.text: What idea ties together Locke, the colonists who protested the Stamp Act, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man?

answers.text: A king may rule as he wishes if he is chosen by the Church.
Government rests on consent and must protect the people's rights.
Government should be run only by those who own the most land.
The people may never resist a government that keeps order.

questions.feedback_correct: Locke published his Treatises in 1689. The colonists replied that they could not be taxed without their consent.

questions.text: Montesquieu, Rousseau, Robespierre, and Bolívar all thought about what free government needs. What do the lessons conclude?

answers.text: Good laws need good habits, which force cannot create.
Good laws alone are enough to keep a people free.
A strong leader can teach virtue quickly through fear.
Habits matter little once a constitution is written.

questions.feedback_correct: Habits grow slowly through families, churches, and schools. Bolívar learned how hard it is to build free government without them.

questions.text: Louis XIV, Napoleon, Bismarck's Germany, and the Kaiser each led other powers to join against the strongest. What principle is this?

answers.text: The divine right of kings.
The separation of powers.
The balance of power.
The invisible hand.

questions.feedback_correct: When one state grows strong enough to dominate its neighbors, the others unite against it.

questions.text: Napoleon's armies, the revolutions of 1848, Italy, Germany, and Versailles all involved nationalism. What do the lessons show?

answers.text: It was a weak force that disappeared after the revolutions of 1848.
It was powerful but hard to satisfy, leaving many minorities.
It was easy to satisfy once each people had a king of its own.
It was a force that only Germans and Italians ever felt.

questions.feedback_correct: The shape of the new states depended on particular decisions. After 1919, millions were left in states ruled by another nation.

questions.text: Cortés, Clive, and the Europeans in Africa all used local people. What does this show about empire?

answers.text: Conquerors won only by the force of their own weapons.
Local people refused to take any part in the new governments.
Local rulers always gave way as soon as Europeans arrived.
Conquerors relied on local rivals, soldiers, and workers.

questions.feedback_correct: Native allies were most of Cortés's army, sepoys fought for the Company, and Africans did most of the work of building roads and railways.

questions.text: Smith, Marx, Stalin's Five-Year Plan, and the collapse of communism all concern who decides what is made. Which statement fits the lessons?

answers.text: Markets made everyone better off, and no worker ever lost a job.
Planned economies made more goods than markets and avoided every cost.
Both systems worked equally well in every country and every period.
Planners lacked price signals, while markets made wealth at some cost.

questions.feedback_correct: Planners could not know what millions wanted. The lesson on globalization notes that a worker whose job moves abroad may lose it.

questions.text: Napoleon, Lenin, Stalin, and Hitler each built a regime around one man or one party. What weakness do the lessons name?

answers.text: These regimes depended on free elections and a free press.
They rested on one will and shut out peaceful ways to settle quarrels.
These regimes were weak because they gave too much power to parliaments.
These regimes were short-lived because the people rose against them at once.

questions.feedback_correct: A free republic needs ways to settle quarrels peacefully, and the Terror had destroyed them.

questions.text: From the sugar plantation to Haiti to abolition, which statement fits the course?

answers.text: Sugar bred bondage, the enslaved resisted, and abolition took decades.
Sugar was grown only by free workers, and the trade ended in 1700.
Abolition came at once, when Parliament heard the first petition.
The enslaved took no part in ending slavery, which was done by kings.

questions.feedback_correct: Haiti declared independence in 1804. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and abolished slavery in 1833.

questions.text: Spanish silver, Philip II's bankruptcies, and Louis XVI's debt show what about wealth and the state?

answers.text: A state that digs up more silver will always grow richer than its rivals.
A state can borrow forever if its king is popular.
Treasure and loans cannot replace production and fair taxes.
A state that has debts will always win its wars.

questions.feedback_correct: A country gets rich by producing things, not by digging up money. France went bankrupt in 1789.

questions.text: The lessons warn against the old story that reason simply marched forward. Which evidence supports that warning?

answers.text: Every Enlightenment writer opposed kings, and no king read their works.
The Enlightenment reached nearly every peasant in Europe within a few years.
Its ideas served absolute monarchs as well as their challengers.
Enlightenment thinkers all agreed on how government should be run.

questions.feedback_correct: Frederick and Catherine used the ideas to reform from above, and revolutionaries later claimed to speak for the general will.

questions.text: Berlin drew Africa's borders, the League gave out mandates, and Radcliffe drew the line in Punjab and Bengal. What do the lessons say about borders drawn by outsiders?

answers.text: They always matched the languages and customs of the people who lived there.
They were quickly redrawn by the peoples themselves, with little trouble.
They had no effect on the new states once independence was won.
They often cut across peoples or joined enemies, leaving lasting problems.

questions.feedback_correct: The new states often inherited borders that cut across peoples and joined enemies, and many soon fell under one-party or military rule.

quizzes.title: A.8 Reading Quiz: Voyages and the Historian's Tools
quizzes.description: This quiz covers Lessons A.1 and A.2. It has 7 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: The Portuguese caravel could sail against the wind better than older ships. Why did this matter so much on the African coast?

answers.text: Pirates hid in the bays along the coast and chased slow ships back out to sea.
Harbors there were too shallow for any ship with large square sails to enter safely.
Winds there blow south, so a ship that sailed south easily still needed a way to get home.
African rulers would trade only with captains whose ships could leave in a single day.

questions.feedback_correct: The coastal winds pushed ships south. A ship that could work against the wind, and a pilot who found the westerlies far out in the Atlantic, could come home with news and cargo.

questions.text: Portugal's royal advisors told the king not to pay for Columbus's plan. What did they believe?

answers.text: Asia lay much farther west than Columbus claimed, so the voyage would run out of food.
The Atlantic was already claimed by Spain, and a Portuguese ship would be seized.
Columbus was too old to command a fleet and would be unable to hire a crew.
A sea route to Asia already existed around Africa, so a western route was needless.

questions.feedback_correct: Columbus believed the earth was much smaller than it is. The experts were right about its size, which is why the plan looked reckless to them.

questions.text: Dias reached the southern tip of Africa in 1488 and da Gama reached India ten years later. What did Dias's voyage make possible?

answers.text: It proved that the Spice Islands lay close enough to Lisbon to reach without stopping.
It gave Portugal a legal claim to all of Asia under the Treaty of Tordesillas.
It showed that the Indian Ocean lay open beyond the Cape, so a sea road to Asia could exist.
It showed that the Pacific could be crossed from the African coast in a single season.

questions.feedback_correct: Once Dias had rounded the Cape and found open water, the question became whether a fleet could cross the Indian Ocean. Da Gama answered it.

questions.text: In 1609 the Dutch East India Company hired Henry Hudson to look for a northern route to Asia. What change in sponsorship does this show?

answers.text: Companies that raised money from many investors now paid for voyages alongside kings.
Kings were no longer interested in the spice trade and left exploration to private groups.
The Dutch crown gave up its claim to the sea in return for a share of all profits.
Captains now had to be citizens of the nation that sponsored the voyage they led.

questions.feedback_correct: Early voyages were funded by crowns. By Hudson's day, merchants pooling money in chartered companies were ready to gamble on distant ventures.

questions.text: Ramadan falls in summer in some years and in winter in others. What explains this?

answers.text: The Islamic calendar counts years from a different starting date than the Christian one.
A lunar year is about eleven days shorter than a solar year, so lunar months drift through the seasons.
Muslims move the month by decision of the community each year to suit the harvest.
The month of fasting was set by early rulers to match the changing length of daylight.

questions.feedback_correct: The Islamic calendar is purely lunar and never adds a month to catch up with the sun, so each month slides earlier through the seasons by about eleven days a year.

questions.text: England did not adopt the Gregorian calendar until 1752, nearly two centuries after Catholic countries did. Which explanation fits the lesson best?

answers.text: The reform came from a pope, and Protestant England was unwilling to follow him.
English astronomers had proved that the older calendar was in fact more accurate.
English farmers needed the extra ten days to finish the harvest before the winter.
The English king feared that dropping days would make people late in paying taxes.

questions.feedback_correct: The text says Protestant England and its colonies resisted for 170 years. The correction was sound, but it carried a pope's name.

questions.text: Archaeologists found Richard III's skeleton under a parking lot in 2012. Why did identifying him take both documents and science?

answers.text: Radiocarbon dating alone gave his exact name, and the documents only agreed with it.
The skeleton had been moved many times, so no one could tie it to a place.
Documents pointed to the friary site, and dating and DNA confirmed the man.
Old chronicles were all lost, so only DNA could say where he had been buried.

questions.feedback_correct: Chronicles said where he was buried. The dig, radiocarbon dating, and a DNA match with a descendant of his family confirmed who the skeleton was.

quizzes.title: A.9 Reading Quiz: Reform and Atrocity
quizzes.description: This quiz covers Lessons A.3 and A.4. It has 7 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: In 1975 Prime Minister Indira Gandhi jailed opponents and censored the press. In 1977 she called an election, lost, and left office. What does this show about India's democracy?

answers.text: Democracy survived partly because a powerful leader chose to obey the voters.
Her party was too weak to hold power, so the army removed her without a vote.
Elections in India were always so one-sided that no leader needed to worry.
The courts forced her out, and she had no say in the matter at all.

questions.feedback_correct: India's parties, election commission, and press all mattered. So did her decision to accept a defeat she could have refused.

questions.text: Ghana began as a parliamentary democracy under Nkrumah but within a few years was a one-party state. How did this make the later coup easier to carry out?

answers.text: He gave the army so much power by law that it could dismiss any elected official.
He sold the nation's gold abroad, and soldiers were no longer being paid by anyone.
He had silenced the opposition, so there was no lawful way to remove him.
He banned the army and left the country with no force able to defend the government.

questions.feedback_correct: With opposition parties banned and critics in jail, the ballot box could not change the government. That left force as the only remaining way.

questions.text: In 1988 Chileans voted on whether Pinochet should rule for eight more years. Which combination best explains why the vote led to real change?

answers.text: The opposition united and watched the count, and Pinochet accepted the result.
A foreign army stood at the border and forced the general to accept the count.
The vote was secret, so Pinochet never learned how most people had voted.
The junta had already planned to step down and used the vote to announce it.

questions.feedback_correct: Parties that had been divided joined together and registered millions of voters. Pinochet had expected to win but kept his word when he lost.

questions.text: Tiananmen in 1989, Myanmar in 1990, and Egypt in 2013 ended badly for reformers. What did these cases share?

answers.text: Each country's people had little interest in a change of government at all.
One institution, the army or a single party, held more power than any rival could check.
Each country had too many political parties for any one to govern the nation.
Each country was invaded by a neighbor soon after the reformers took power.

questions.feedback_correct: In the successes, parties, churches, newspapers, and unions could check a ruler. In these failures one armed institution outweighed all of them.

questions.text: A war that kills a great many people is not necessarily a genocide. What does the definition of genocide turn on?

answers.text: Whether the killing was done by a government instead of by a rebel army.
Whether more than one million people died, counting both soldiers and civilians.
Whether the aim was to destroy a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group as such.
Whether foreign nations had signed a treaty to stay out of the fighting.

questions.feedback_correct: Intent is the key. A war with great loss of life may be a tragedy and a crime without being genocide, which is why the label is often argued over.

questions.text: Most of the Khmer Rouge's victims were fellow Khmer, yet a court in 2018 convicted two leaders of genocide against the Vietnamese and the Cham. Why does this still leave lawyers debating the label for the whole slaughter?

answers.text: The court could not find that any killing had taken place in Cambodia.
Most victims were not from a group the Khmer Rouge targeted as a national or ethnic group.
The convicted men had served in the army and were not responsible for any killing.
Vietnam had already tried the leaders and the court was unable to try them again.

questions.feedback_correct: The finding of genocide covered particular groups. Whether the mass killing of the rest of the population fits the same legal definition is still argued.

questions.text: Belgium gave every Rwandan an identity card stating his group. How did this later help the killers of 1994?

answers.text: It gave them the legal right under Belgian law to take the land of the Tutsi.
It taught young Rwandans to read, and so made radio broadcasts easier to spread.
It ended the old kingdom and with it every law that had once protected the Tutsi.
It fixed a loose difference into an official label that told them whom to target.

questions.feedback_correct: Rwanda's two groups shared one language and one land. A card that named each person's group made it easy to pick out victims when the killing began.

quizzes.title: A.10 Reading Quiz: Radicals and Religion in Russia
quizzes.description: This quiz covers Lesson A.5. It has 6 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: Radicals killed Tsar Alexander II in 1881, and his son answered with harsher rule. Why was this an irony?

answers.text: The tsar's son had secretly supported the radicals and then betrayed them.
The radicals were all executed, so none of them lived to see the result.
The murdered tsar was the reformer, and the response ended moderate reforms.
The assassins were pardoned, and the tsar's own guards were punished instead.

questions.feedback_correct: Alexander II had freed the serfs and created courts and local councils. His death brought Alexander III, a larger secret police, and a harder line.

questions.text: In 1874 thousands of students went to the villages to teach the peasants and stir them to revolt. Many were turned over to the police. What does this suggest about the peasants?

answers.text: They were pious and loyal to the tsar and distrusted the students' message.
They had already begun a revolt and did not need the help of the students.
They could not hear the students, who spoke only in a foreign language.
They wanted the landlords punished but feared the students would do the same.

questions.feedback_correct: The populists' trust in the people was misplaced. Many concluded that talk was useless and only force would work.

questions.text: Lenin said that workers by themselves would only ask for better wages. What did he conclude they needed?

answers.text: A free press that could tell the whole country what the tsar was doing.
Leaders who would be chosen by all party members in a public vote.
A small, strict party of full-time revolutionaries to lead them.
A parliament in which every class could argue its case in the open.

questions.feedback_correct: This was the idea of the vanguard. It drew on the Russian tradition of secret circles and underground work.

questions.text: The Bolsheviks did not cause the February revolution of 1917, yet they took power in October. What gave them the advantage?

answers.text: Discipline and experience in underground work while the new government was weak.
Their huge membership, which easily outnumbered every other party in the country.
The support of the army, which had been won over by a long civil war.
A secret treaty with Germany that gave them money and soldiers to use.

questions.feedback_correct: Hunger, defeat in war, and the fall of the tsar caused the first revolution. A tightly run party ready to act then filled the vacuum.

questions.text: Why did the Soviet government treat the Russian Orthodox Church as a danger?

answers.text: It was the largest group outside party control, with a loyalty beyond the state.
Its priests had led an army that tried to put the tsar back on the throne.
Its clergy refused to pay taxes and spent all their wealth on missions abroad.
Its churches stood on land that the state wanted for new factories and roads.

questions.feedback_correct: A government that wanted total control saw any rival loyalty as a threat, and the Church was by far the largest.

questions.text: In 1943 Stalin allowed the Church to choose a patriarch. What does the timing suggest?

He needed every ally in the war with Germany and eased the pressure for that reason.
He had given up his belief in atheism after reading the Bible during the war.
The Church had agreed to give all of its remaining land and property to the state.

questions.feedback_correct: The policy bent to the needs of the war. Another harsh campaign closed thousands of churches under Khrushchev around 1960.

quizzes.title: A.11 Reading Quiz: Regions and Migration
quizzes.description: This quiz covers Lessons A.6 and A.7. It has 7 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: The Sahel has thin, uncertain rainfall. Which pair shows a physical trait leading to a human trait there?

answers.text: Dense forest leading to fishing villages and large sea-going trading ships.
Tall mountains leading to terraced rice fields and a wet monsoon each year.
A cold climate leading to a dependence on timber and on iron smelted from bog ore.
Dry grassland leading to herding, millet farming, and caravan trade across the desert.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson shows regions defined by both kinds of trait, and the human ones often grow from the physical ones.

questions.text: Argentina was among the richest countries in 1900 and fell well behind, while South Korea went from poverty to wealth in two generations. What does this suggest?

answers.text: Choices by governments and citizens matter as much as geography does.
Countries with a long coast can never remain poor for more than a few decades.
Wealth depends only on the amount of oil or gold found beneath the ground.
Poor countries become rich only after they have been ruled by a foreign power.

questions.feedback_correct: Neither country's position changed. Their laws, policies, and habits did, which is why geography sets the scene but does not write the play.

questions.text: Why does Egypt fear the Ethiopian dam on the Blue Nile more than Ethiopia fears any Egyptian response?

answers.text: Ethiopia's land lies at sea level and cannot be damaged by changes in the water flow.
Egypt is nearly all desert and relies on the river for almost all its fresh water.
Egypt has no army, and Ethiopia has promised to attack any country that objects.
Egypt has no way to build dams of its own and must buy all of its electricity.

questions.feedback_correct: Most of Egypt's people live on a narrow strip beside the Nile. A drop in the river's flow hits them directly, while Ethiopia sees the dam as a way out of poverty.

questions.text: The Aral Sea shrank after the 1960s. Who bore most of the harm?

answers.text: Sailors on the open ocean, who lost the shipping lanes of the Persian Gulf.
People living near the old shore, though a distant government made the choice.
The Soviet planners, who lost their cotton fields in a sudden flood.
Farmers in the mountains, who saw their rivers fill with salt from the sea.

questions.feedback_correct: The cotton brought income, but the dry lake bed sent salty dust over nearby fields and homes, and the people nearest it paid the price.

questions.text: Which pair names a push factor and a pull factor in the Irish migration after 1845?

answers.text: The failure of the potato crop pushed people out, and better wages in America pulled them across.
Heavy taxes on grain pushed people out, and the cheap land in Canada pulled them across.
British soldiers pushed people out, and the free passage on Royal Navy ships pulled them across.
A lack of schools pushed people out, and the chance of a university degree pulled them across.

questions.feedback_correct: Hunger from the blight was the push. The pull was jobs on canals, railroads, and in factories, at far higher pay than at home.

questions.text: West Germany expected its Turkish guest workers to stay a year or two, yet millions of their descendants are German citizens today. Which explanation fits best?

answers.text: The workers had been promised German citizenship before they arrived.
Turkey stopped accepting them back when the economy there slowed down.
Many stayed after recruiting ended in 1973 and brought their families.
Germany forced them to stay by closing its borders in 1961.

questions.feedback_correct: The stay was meant to be temporary. Wages kept people in Germany, and the families who followed built new lives and neighborhoods there.

questions.text: Ciudad Juarez grew into a city of more than a million after 1965. What best explains the growth?

answers.text: A program let foreign factories build near the border, so workers moved north for jobs.
Mexico's government moved its capital there to be nearer its northern neighbor.
A great famine in the south forced the people of every village to migrate north.
A ban on trade across the river made Juarez a safe haven for refugees from Texas.

questions.feedback_correct: The maquiladora factories drew workers from all over Mexico. The twin cities on the border now depend on each other for trade and family ties.

quizzes.title: A.12 Module Test: Supplementary Lessons
quizzes.description: This test covers all seven lessons in this module. It has 14 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text: The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 drew a line down the Atlantic. What was its purpose?

answers.text: To set the limits of the fishing waters that Portugal shared with England.
To keep Spain and Portugal from fighting over the lands they were finding.
To end the war between Spain and Portugal over the kingdom of Granada.
To divide the Pacific between the two nations after Magellan's voyage.

questions.feedback_correct: Spain could claim lands to the west of the line, and Portugal to the east.

questions.text: Only one of Magellan's five ships returned to Spain, yet the voyage still mattered. What did it show?

answers.text: That cloves could not be grown in the Americas and had to be imported.
That the earth could be circled by sea and that the Pacific was vastly large.
That Portugal's route around Africa was too dangerous for regular use.
That the Atlantic was too wide for any further trade between Spain and Asia.

questions.feedback_correct: The fleet lost most of its men and ships, but the survivors proved the earth could be circled and that the Pacific was far larger than anyone in Europe had guessed.

questions.text: Plutarch wrote his Parallel Lives to show Greek and Roman statesmen at their best and worst. What did he think history was?

answers.text: A record of treaties and laws whose dates a student ought to memorize.
A school of character, in which a reader learns how to act by watching others.
A set of cycles in which every empire must rise and fall in the same way.
A form of poetry meant to praise the rulers who paid for the books.

questions.feedback_correct: Plutarch held up great men as models and warnings. Founders of later republics read him in that spirit.

questions.text: The French revolutionaries' ten-day week was abolished by Napoleon in 1806. What does its failure suggest about calendars?

answers.text: A calendar must be based on the moon, or else it cannot serve a modern nation.
Governments can change a calendar only after a successful war abroad.
A calendar tied to worship and habit is hard for a government to change by order.
A calendar that begins from a new year number will always be thrown out.

questions.feedback_correct: The ten-day week gave people fewer days of rest and cut across the calendar of saints and Sundays. A calendar is bound up with a people's habits.

questions.text: In 1986 Marcos claimed victory in the Philippines despite evidence of fraud. Why did he fall?

answers.text: The courts of his own country ruled that he could not stay in office.
His own party held a secret vote and replaced him with another leader.
Soldiers refused to fire on the peaceful crowds that filled the main avenue.
Foreign troops entered Manila and took control of the main government buildings.

questions.feedback_correct: Hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, and when the soldiers would not fire, the regime had nothing left to rely on.

questions.text: Nelson Mandela served only one term as president of South Africa. What example did this set?

answers.text: It showed that a president could rule only if every party had an equal vote.
It showed that a leader can give up power peacefully and build trust.
It showed that foreign governments chose the leaders of the new nation.
It showed that the army held the true power and the president was a figurehead.

questions.feedback_correct: A peaceful handing on of power helped the new democracy to take root, and it could have ended in civil war.

questions.text: Srebrenica was declared a safe area by the United Nations, yet more than eight thousand men and boys were killed there. What made this possible?

answers.text: The town was far outside the area patrolled by any peacekeeper from any nation.
The United Nations had withdrawn its force a month earlier and left the town empty.
Dutch peacekeepers there had few soldiers and orders not to fight.
The Bosnian army had been ordered to hand over the town to the Bosnian Serbs.

questions.feedback_correct: A declaration of safety meant little without the force to defend it.

questions.text: General Roméo Dallaire asked for more troops as the killing in Rwanda began. How did the Security Council respond?

answers.text: It sent a larger force within a week that stopped the killing in the capital.
It ordered the rebel army to withdraw from the capital until a vote was held.
It ended all talk of the war and left the matter to Belgium alone to settle.
It cut the size of the force that was already there.

questions.feedback_correct: The small UN force was reduced when it was most needed. The killing stopped when the Tutsi-led rebel army took the capital in July.

questions.text: The Decembrists failed in a single day in 1825. Why do they matter to the story of Russian radicals?

answers.text: Their example and their wives' loyalty became a legend for later radicals.
Their plan became the model for the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917.
They won a constitution that every later tsar was required to respect.
They founded the first political party in Russia to hold regular elections.

questions.feedback_correct: Five leaders were hanged and many others sent to Siberia, but the memory of the revolt inspired generations who came after.

questions.text: In 1967 Albania did something no other state had done. What was it?

answers.text: It allowed each region to choose its own religion and to tax its followers.
It gave its churches and mosques to the state and let believers use them in secret.
It declared itself an officially atheist state after closing most places of worship.
It signed a treaty with the Soviet Union that put its clergy under Moscow's control.

questions.feedback_correct: Albania closed or destroyed most of its churches and mosques and then declared itself the first officially atheist state.

questions.text: Why does the Strait of Hormuz matter to countries thousands of miles from the Persian Gulf?

answers.text: Much of the world's seaborne oil must pass through one narrow channel.
The strait is the only place where ships can cross from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
The countries on the Gulf control most of the world's supply of fresh water.
The strait is the only route by which wheat can reach the cities of East Asia.

questions.feedback_correct: A channel about twenty-one miles wide at its narrowest carries oil tankers to Europe and East Asia, so whoever controls it can threaten faraway economies.

questions.text: Countries without a seacoast, such as Mali and Chad, tend to be poorer. Which reason does the lesson give?

answers.text: They have no deserts, and so their land is too wet to farm in most years.
Trade costs more because their goods must cross other countries to reach a port.
Their people are not allowed to leave and so cannot learn from other nations.
They have no rivers, and so they cannot grow food for their people.

questions.feedback_correct: Physical conditions are one of several causes. Land-locked countries pay more to trade, and history and politics matter too.

questions.text: The 1947 partition of India divided Punjab. What was one effect?

answers.text: Every village in the region became home to a mix of Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs.
Cities only about thirty miles apart ended up on opposite sides of a hostile border.
The two halves of Punjab joined into a single province under Pakistani rule.
The region's farmers all moved east to the cities of Bengal and Assam.

questions.feedback_correct: Lahore and Amritsar were split by the new line. Millions crossed it in both directions, and many died.

questions.text: In 2015 many Syrian refugees traveled on to Europe. What was the effect on border areas such as the Greek islands and the Balkan roads?

answers.text: They became crowded, and governments quarreled over who should carry the load.
They were closed to all trade by order of the United Nations Security Council.
They emptied out, since no one wished to live near so many travelers.
They grew rich from the tolls that the migrants paid at each crossing.

questions.feedback_correct: A border is a place where pushes and pulls meet, and the pressure fell hardest on the places closest to it.

WEEK 30 · DISCUSSION
Was Imperialism About Profit, Power, or Duty?
Imperialism
💬 DISCUSSION PROMPT

Merchants wanted markets and raw materials. Governments wanted naval bases and prestige. Missionaries and humanitarians wanted to spread the Gospel and to end the slave trade. WEEK 32 · DISCUSSION
Was the Treaty of Versailles Too Harsh or Too Weak?
The Settlement and the Dictators
💬 DISCUSSION PROMPT

Germans called the treaty a dictated peace, and the war guilt clause, the reparations, and the limits on their army stung. Yet Germany lost no factories to invasion and remained the strongest nation in Europe, and the French thought the treaty too weak. The lessons also show a Great Depression, a hyperinflation, and a handful of decisions by men in Berlin and Rome.

WEEK 33 · DISCUSSION
Could Britain and France Have Stopped Hitler in 1938?
World War II and the Holocaust
💬 DISCUSSION PROMPT

discussions.title: 35.6 Discussion: Partition: Could India Have Stayed United?
discussions.html:
WEEK 35 · DISCUSSION
Partition: Could India Have Stayed United?
Decolonization and Israel
💬 DISCUSSION PROMPT

About one in four Indians was Muslim, and many Muslims feared being a permanent minority in a state ruled by a Hindu majority. Jinnah demanded a separate homeland. Gandhi and Nehru opposed dividing the country. Britain decided to leave, set an early date, and gave a lawyer who had never seen India a few weeks to draw the borders. The partition set off one of the largest migrations in history, and hundreds of thousands died.

Is Globalization Uniting or Dividing the World?
The Modern World

Trade, shipping containers, the internet, and shared science have tied the world together and lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty.
